title: Critical Childhood Studies
description: This seminar/capstone course on critical childhood studies will examine the burgeoning field of childhood studies across time periods and regions, employing varied disciplinary approaches to the study of childhood, including literary studies, history, art history, sociology, and other disciplines. Assignments will include weekly responses, leading a discussion of a scholarly work, a final paper on a subject related to student interest, and a presentation of the final paper topic.

title: Cognitive Poetics
description: This course is designed to enable students to use cognitive neuroscience to read world literature. It is centered around two general issues: how our hunter-gatherer brain supports the production of a wide range of literature and how the study of literature, in turn, can be used to understand our species cognitive design. This approach introduces students to cutting-edge interdisciplinary research. Studying literature from across the globe together with cognitive neuroscience also explains how universal cognitive capacities actually support local environmental variations in language, script and genre. Students can use this foundational survey course to take specialized classes on literature and emotion, and storytelling and the mind.

title: From Superman to Spiegelman: The Jewish Graphic Novel
description: This survey of graphic novels by Jewish authors will include selections of early comics, works by American authors such as Eisner, Spiegelman, and Pekar, and Israeli graphic novels. The seminar-style discussions will address varied themes, including identity, gender, trauma and memory.

title: Photography and Religion
description: Offers an examination of the relationship between religion and photography through history, based on the consideration of photography as both an artistic medium and a social and performative practice. Alongside analysis of the function of photographs in religious life, we will explore various religious concepts in association with photography. Through meditations on topics as spirit, death, ritual, iconicity, sacred space, and gender, students will become familiar with critical theory of photography, visual analysis, and landmark photographs.

title: Identity, Feminism, and Secularism in Hebrew Literature
description: Provides a broad overview of Modern Hebrew literature, spanning from its origins in the eighteenth century to the contemporary era. Aims to shed light on the factors that make this literature distinctive and fascinating. The course delves into various themes, such as Jewish identity, feminism, secularism, and Zionism, while examining the interplay and conflicts between different generations of literary works. The readings for the course comprise a selection of short stories in translation, but will be available in Hebrew for interested students. All lectures and discussions will be held in English.

title: Major Works in German Literature: Kafka
description: A selection of Franz Kafka's novels, short stories and diaries will be closely read and analyzed. Readings, lecture and discussion in English.

title: Science and Technology in European Philosophy
description: Introduces various positions from the history and present of European philosophy that speak to questions of science and technology. Readings may include Aristotle, Descartes, Kant, Nietzsche, Freud, Heidegger, Arendt, Bachelard, Koyr, Caillois, Foucault, Canguilhem, Blumenberg, Serres, Malabou, Stiegler. Topics may include: machine theories, cybernetics, structuralism in science, techniques of simulation, artificial intelligence.

title: Interdisciplinary Comparative Literature Studies
description: Interdisciplinary examination of selected topics, theories, disciplinary issues, and/or methodological questions in the combined study of literature, and other areas of the humanities and humanistic sciences. Course focus will be determined by the instructor(s).

title: Moving Bodies: Stories of Migration
description: Moving Bodies: Stories of Migration. Examines the experience of migration by focusing on how the Basques settled in the American West.

title: Adultery in the Novel
description: Marriage and adultery in Western narratives. We explore narrative techniques as well as relations between love, law, and gender. Readings include 19th-century novels from Europe and Brazil.

title: Gender in Basque Culture
description: Using Basque culture as a case study, this course explores how gender intersects with other crucial issues such as ethnicity, nationhood, and globalization.

title: The Aftermath of Enlightenment
description: Introduces the critical study of biography before examining Buddha's life as the foundation of all Buddhist biographies. Then considers Tibetan accounts of life after enlightenment, from chaste monks to drunken tantrikas, to discuss Buddhist ethics and narrative expressions of reality.

title: Bulgakov
description: Intensive study of Bulgakov. Readings supplemented by selected criticism. Taught in English.

title: The Basques Through Film
description: The Basques through Film. Provides a critical examination of the history and poetics of Basque film from the last three decades.

title: Interdisciplinary Comparative Literature Studies
description: Interdisciplinary examination of selected topics, theories, disciplinary issues, and/or methodological questions in the combined study of literature, and other areas of the humanities and humanistic sciences. Course focus will be determined by the instructor(s).

title: Documentary Filmmaking & Democracy
description: Documentary films and the advent of democracy in the late twentieth century. Topics include the exploration of the effect of technology on documentary film as an aesthetic form, a material medium, and an ideological construct.

title: Conflict and Memory in Cultural Production
description: Conflict, Memory and Cultural Production. Explores how Basque writers and artists engage and create memory narratives in times of war and violence.

title: Basque Studies Through Literature and Culture in Translation (Spanish/English)
description: The course delves deeper into the diversity of topics that make up Basque Studies, analyzing historical, but also contemporary socio-cultural topics related to the Basque Country and the Basque diaspora abroad. The course can be taken either as a continuation of SPAN 153E or a self-standing course on Basque Studies, where literary and cultural materials will be presented in their English, Spanish, and possibly also French translations depending on student interest and language choice.

title: Exile, Displacement, and Estrangement in Literature and Film
description: A focus on contemporary representations of exile and displacement, and exiled authors and thinkers from Latin America and Europe. Primary sources include texts about European exiles in the Americas, Latin American exiles in Europe, and the turn from exile to migrant literature in the Americas. We also look to how contemporary authors adapt early exile motifs and respond to literary forerunners by including issues of gender, labor, racism, sexuality, and more.

title: NOIR: 1940's Film and Fiction
description: Focuses on learning the terminology, historical context, and main theories that will help develop an informed understanding of film noir as a narrative film genre.

title: Vegetarianism: Food, Literature, Philosophy
description: The philosophical, religious and literary history of vegetarianism and animal ethics from the Antiquity to the present. Topics include the debate on animal consumption in the Buddhist canon and recent representations of vegetarianism in western literature.

title: Interdisciplinary Comparative Literature Studies
description: Interdisciplinary examination of selected topics, theories, disciplinary issues, and/or methodological questions in the combined study of literature, and other areas of the humanities and humanistic sciences. Course focus will be determined by the instructor(s).

title: Iceland's Folklore and Witchcraft
description: Intensive two-week summer course taught in Iceland offering an overview of how concepts of magic, wisdom, knowledge of the world and the occult shaped folklore, society, and material culture in Iceland compared with similar phenomena elsewhere, and covering from the Middle Ages to the post-reformation era (17th & 18th centuries), and up to the early 20th century. Through readings (in translation) and field trips around the island, students will investigate traditional dwellings, rituals, burials, production of food and commodities, human interactions with the harsh natural environment, and the effects these activities and places had on culture and beliefs, including ghosts, revenants, elves, and trolls.

title: Dostoevsky
description: Intensive study of Dostoevsky. Readings supplemented by select criticism. Readings and lectures in English.
